lessons.title: Elizabeth I: background, character and the royal court

before.exam_tip_html: For an ‘Explain Effects’ question on Elizabeth’s court or character, name a specific consequence and link it to a named individual or event — not a vague ‘the country was united’. For example: ‘Patronage of Robert Dudley as Master of the Horse meant Elizabeth had a loyal courtier inside her Privy Chamber.’ Markers reward precise causal links over general description.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Elizabeth I’s royal court.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The court was a travelling household of around 1,500 people that moved between palaces such as Whitehall and Hampton Court and made summer progresses through nobles’ estates.
• Access to the queen was tightly controlled through the Privy Chamber, where only senior ministers and favourites such as Robert Dudley could meet her in private.
• Patronage — appointments, monopolies, lands and titles — was distributed at court, binding ambitious nobles and gentry to the Crown.
• Court ritual and image-making, including portraits and processions, performed Elizabeth’s authority in public.
[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for a developed feature with supporting detail.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of patronage on Elizabeth’s control of the nobility between 1568 and 1603.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Patronage allowed Elizabeth to reward loyal nobles with lands, monopolies and offices, binding them to the Crown without the expense of a standing army.
• It set rivals against each other — Cecil against Leicester, then Robert Cecil against Essex — so ambitious men competed for the queen’s favour rather than combining against her.
• It extended royal authority into the counties, since Lord-Lieutenancies and Justice-of-the-Peace appointments were used to manage local militia and the law.
• When patronage broke down — Essex losing his sweet wine monopoly in 1600 — it directly contributed to rebellion, showing the system’s limits.

Mastering: Multiple effects developed with named individuals and a clear causal chain.
Secure: Two or more effects explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple points; little development.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Elizabeth’s upbringing and education for her reign after 1568.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Her humanist education in Latin, Greek and theology gave her the confidence to argue directly with ministers and bishops — visible in later disputes with Parliament over the succession.
• Her imprisonment in the Tower under Mary I taught caution and secrecy, which shaped her habit of delaying decisions on marriage and war.
• Her popular touch — cultivated during her uncertain youth — helped her play the role of ‘Gloriana’ on progresses and in speeches.
• Significance over time: these qualities supported a 45-year reign in which a Protestant female ruler survived plots, excommunication and the Armada.

Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and over time, with precise examples.
Secure: Clear significance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance with limited examples.
Emerging: Simple description; significance unclear.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Elizabethan court patronage.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Monopolies on traded goods such as sweet wines were granted to favourites, allowing them to charge a fee on imports.
• Appointments such as Lord-Lieutenancies and Justices of the Peace gave nobles authority over county militia and law in return for loyalty.
• Court favourites such as Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, gained access to the Privy Chamber, the most valuable form of patronage.
• Lesser gentry and clients reached the Crown through chains of intermediaries — for example, through Burghley’s household.
[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for development.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Elizabeth’s character on her style of government.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Caution and delay — on marriage and on intervention abroad — meant the regime avoided rash commitments but frustrated ministers and Parliament.
• Public image-making (the Rainbow and Armada portraits, progresses) projected authority that compensated for the absence of an heir or husband.
• Her temper inside court (slapping courtiers, throwing a shoe at Walsingham) reminded ministers that final authority lay with her.
• Her humanist learning allowed her to dominate council debate and theology arguments, reinforcing her personal control.

Mastering: Effects clearly developed with specific examples and consequences.
Secure: Two or more effects with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified, limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; effects unclear.

practice_questions.text: Argue, using examples from across Elizabeth’s reign, that personal monarchy — rather than ministers or Parliament — was the most important factor in how England was governed between 1568 and 1603.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include arguments in support:
• Patronage flowed from the queen personally; lands, monopolies and offices were her gift, which bound nobles to the Crown.
• Elizabeth’s caution, image-making and personal authority over the court controlled the speed and direction of policy — for example, refusing to name an heir for 45 years.
• Even her ministers’ power depended on her favour: Burghley remained influential because she trusted him, and Essex fell when she withdrew patronage.

Arguments to weigh against:
• William Cecil and Walsingham ran day-to-day government and intelligence; without their administration the regime would not have functioned.
• Parliament granted taxation and passed laws (e.g. the religious settlement and Poor Laws) that the Crown depended on.
• Local government — Justices of the Peace, county gentry — enforced law without direct royal supervision.

A strong response weighs personal monarchy against ministerial and parliamentary contributions and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Mastering: Sustained argument across the period with embedded evidence and a justified judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence on both sides.
Developing: Some argument; evidence may be limited.
Emerging: Simple points; little argument or judgement.

lessons.title: Key ministers: Cecil, Walsingham and the Privy Council

before.content_html:
Why Ministers Mattered

Elizabeth set policy, but she could not run a kingdom of four million people on her own. Her power depended on a small group of ministers who managed finance, foreign policy, the law, intelligence and the day-to-day flow of royal correspondence. Three names dominate this story: William Cecil (Lord Burghley), Sir Francis Walsingham, and Cecil’s son Robert. Together with the wider Privy Council, they were the engine room of the regime.

William Cecil (Lord Burghley)

William Cecil served Elizabeth from 1558, the day she became queen, until his death in 1598 — almost the entire reign. He was first her Principal Secretary, then from 1572 Lord Treasurer (chief finance minister), and was made Lord Burghley in 1571. Cecil’s strengths were administration and patience. He kept meticulous notes, drafted memoranda weighing up the pros and cons of every option, and waited for Elizabeth’s decision rather than forcing her hand. The historian John Guy has called him ‘the indispensable man’ of the regime.

Cecil was a moderate Protestant who believed England’s safety required peace abroad and stability at home. He pushed for the execution of Mary, Queen of Scots, but only after years of building a legal and political case. He resisted ruinously expensive wars but agreed when threats — such as the Spanish Armada — could no longer be avoided. He trained his younger son Robert to take over from him, and on Burghley’s death in 1598 the transition was almost seamless.

Key Fact

William Cecil (Lord Burghley) was Principal Secretary 1558–1572 and Lord Treasurer 1572–1598 — almost the entire reign. He was the administrator who turned Elizabeth’s decisions into working policy and prepared his son Robert to succeed him.

Sir Francis Walsingham, Spymaster

If Burghley was the manager, Walsingham was the watchman. Appointed Principal Secretary in 1573, he ran what we would now call an intelligence service. Walsingham was a hard Protestant who believed Catholic Europe — especially Spain — was an existential threat to Elizabethan England. He recruited informants in English Catholic communities, intercepted letters between exiles abroad and plotters at home, and ran double agents inside hostile courts.

His most famous coup was the unmasking of the Babington Plot in 1586. Walsingham’s agents intercepted ciphered letters between the conspirators and Mary, Queen of Scots, decrypted them, and even forged a postscript to draw out further names. The evidence convicted Mary, leading to her execution at Fotheringhay Castle in February 1587. Walsingham died in 1590, exhausted and in debt; the queen had paid him too little for the work he had done.

Walsingham paid agents from his own pocket, partly because the Crown was reluctant to fund spies and partly to keep their identities secret from political rivals. His agents posed as Catholic exiles in Paris and Rome, infiltrated seminaries that were training English priests for missions home, and watched the ports for forbidden books. He developed methods for opening, copying and resealing letters without breaking the wax. Code-breakers including Thomas Phelippes worked in his service. None of this had a formal department; it ran through Walsingham’s personal household.

Robert Cecil

Robert Cecil, Burghley’s younger son, succeeded his father as the queen’s leading minister. Trained from boyhood for the role, he was small, hunchbacked and famously sharp-tongued. Elizabeth nicknamed him her ‘little elf’. From the mid-1590s he managed both domestic administration and the secret negotiations that, after Elizabeth’s death in 1603, would secure the peaceful succession of James VI of Scotland as James I of England. His clash with Essex, who saw the Cecils as rivals blocking his ambition, would set up the rebellion of 1601.

The Privy Council

The Privy Council was the queen’s inner advisory body. Around 19–20 men, all hand-picked, met two or three times a week. They debated foreign policy, military matters, religious enforcement, the granting of monopolies, the management of the harvest and law-and-order issues that came to the Crown. Notes were kept by the Clerk of the Council; decisions were sent out as letters carrying Elizabeth’s authority.

Elizabeth used the Council as a sounding board. She did not always attend meetings; instead, ministers debated, summarised the options for her, and waited for her ruling. She often picked apart their conclusions and demanded more information. This style frustrated councillors but kept ultimate authority firmly in her hands. As historian Penry Williams put it, the Council advised; the queen decided.

The Mary mentioned in this lesson is Mary, Queen of Scots — Elizabeth’s Catholic Stuart cousin, executed in 1587. She is not Mary I (also called Mary Tudor or ‘Bloody Mary’), who was Elizabeth’s half-sister and queen of England 1553–1558. Mary I died ten years before this depth study begins. Mixing them up is one of the most common mistakes in Elizabethan exam answers.

Key Fact

Cecil ran administration and finance; Walsingham ran intelligence and uncovered the Babington Plot of 1586; the Privy Council debated policy and turned the queen’s decisions into instructions sent to officials across the kingdom.
before.exam_tip_html: For an ‘Explain Effects’ question on Elizabeth’s ministers, link a named person to a specific outcome — for example, ‘Walsingham’s interception of the Babington letters provided the legal evidence that condemned Mary in 1587.’ Avoid generic claims that ministers ‘helped the queen rule’; markers want precise causation.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Elizabethan Privy Council.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It had around 19–20 members chosen by the queen, including senior nobles, ministers and officials such as the Lord Treasurer.
• It met two or three times a week to debate foreign policy, religion, the harvest, law and order and the granting of monopolies.
• Its decisions were recorded by the Clerk of the Council and sent out as letters carrying the queen’s authority.
• Elizabeth herself often did not attend; ministers presented options and she ruled on them privately.
[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for development.]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Sir Francis Walsingham’s intelligence network.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Walsingham recruited and paid agents personally, often from his own pocket, posing as Catholic exiles in Paris, Rome and the English seminaries abroad.
• His agents intercepted, copied and decrypted letters; codebreakers such as Thomas Phelippes worked in his service.
• The network unmasked the 1586 Babington Plot by intercepting ciphered messages between Anthony Babington and Mary, Queen of Scots.
• The service ran through Walsingham’s personal household, not as a formal Crown department, leaving him in debt by his death.
[4 marks — 2 marks per feature.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of William Cecil’s long service on the stability of Elizabeth’s government.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• His 40 years in office (Principal Secretary 1558–1572, Lord Treasurer 1572–1598) provided continuity in administration through religious threats, plots and war.
• His careful drafting of options and resistance to expensive wars kept Crown finances stable, so Elizabeth could choose when to fight.
• He trained his son Robert to succeed him, allowing an almost seamless transition in 1598 and protecting policy from disruption.
• His backing for the eventual execution of Mary in 1587 — built on years of legal preparation — removed the Catholic claimant without leaving Elizabeth politically exposed.

Mastering: Multiple effects developed with precise dates and outcomes.
Secure: Two or more effects clearly explained.
Developing: Effects identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Simple statements of Cecil’s importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Walsingham’s uncovering of the Babington Plot in 1586.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It produced the documentary evidence that convicted Mary, Queen of Scots, leading to her execution at Fotheringhay in February 1587.
• It removed the Catholic figurehead around whom plots could form, weakening domestic Catholic conspiracies.
• It hardened Spanish hostility — Philip II saw Mary’s execution as the final justification for invasion, contributing to the launching of the Armada in 1588.
• It demonstrated the value of state intelligence, embedding Walsingham’s methods (interception, code-breaking, agents abroad) as part of how the regime defended itself.

Mastering: Effects developed at the time and over time, with named individuals and dates.
Secure: Effects explained clearly with relevant detail.
Developing: Some effects with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple description of the plot.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Privy Council in Elizabethan government.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Council channelled expert advice on foreign policy, religion and finance to the queen, allowing decisions based on weighed evidence rather than personal whim.
• It turned royal decisions into administration: instructions to Justices of the Peace, county sheriffs and ambassadors carried Council authority.
• Significance over time: the Council shaped major events including the religious settlement, the response to the 1569 Northern Rebellion and the build-up to war with Spain.
• Elizabeth used Council debate strategically — absent from many meetings, she preserved ultimate authority while letting ministers refine the options.

Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and over time, with specific examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance with limited examples.
Emerging: Simple description of meetings.

practice_questions.text: Argue, with examples drawn from across the reign, that ministers and the Privy Council — rather than the queen alone — were responsible for the survival of Elizabethan England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include arguments in support:
• Cecil’s 40-year administration kept finances stable and policy continuous through religious threat, plots and war.
• Walsingham’s intelligence network produced the evidence that condemned Mary in 1587, removing the Catholic claimant.
• The Privy Council co-ordinated the response to the Northern Rebellion, the Armada and Essex’s rebellion, channelling local administration to the centre.
• Robert Cecil’s back-channel negotiations secured a peaceful Stuart succession in 1603.

Arguments to weigh against:
• Patronage flowed from the queen personally; ministers depended on her favour for their offices.
• Elizabeth made the final decisions on marriage, religion and the execution of Mary, often delaying ministers’ preferred options.
• Her image-making and personal authority compensated for the absence of an heir or husband.
• Parliament, county gentry and Justices of the Peace also enforced the regime far from the Council.

A strong response weighs ministerial achievement against the queen’s personal authority and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

lessons.title: A female ruler: Parliament, marriage and the succession

before.content_html:
A Woman on the Throne

A queen ruling alone was unusual in sixteenth-century Europe. Most political theorists, churchmen and Members of Parliament assumed that a woman should be guided by her father, husband or king. The Scottish reformer John Knox had even written a pamphlet in 1558 attacking the ‘monstrous regiment of women’. Elizabeth therefore inherited a problem that her father, Henry VIII, had never faced: many of her own subjects believed her sex unfitted her for the role. How she handled Parliament, the question of marriage, and the succession defined her authority for the next 35 years.

Parliament: Useful but Pushy

Elizabeth needed Parliament. Only Parliament could grant taxation (subsidies) to fund the Crown, and only an Act of Parliament had the legal weight to settle religion or change the law of succession. Yet Parliament also held views Elizabeth disliked. Many MPs were strongly Protestant and wanted further religious reform; many were anxious about the unmarried queen and pressed her to choose a husband or name an heir. Elizabeth’s answer was to call Parliament rarely — only ten times in 45 years — and to limit what it discussed.

Two clashes show the pattern. In 1566, MPs led by Paul Wentworth demanded that Elizabeth either marry or name a successor. She replied that the matter was a matter of prerogative — her decision alone — and forbade discussion. In 1576, Peter Wentworth (Paul’s brother) argued that Parliament had a right to free speech on any subject; he was sent to the Tower. Elizabeth let Parliament grant her money, but on her terms.

Key Fact

Elizabeth called Parliament only ten times between 1559 and 1601. She accepted its right to grant taxation and pass laws but ruled that the queen’s marriage and the succession were matters of royal prerogative and not for MPs to debate.

The Marriage Question

From the day she became queen, ministers and ambassadors expected Elizabeth to marry. A husband would, they assumed, give her political guidance, military support and an heir. Suitors lined up for almost two decades. Philip II of Spain (her dead sister’s husband) proposed within months. Archduke Charles of Austria was considered seriously through the 1560s. King Erik XIV of Sweden sent expensive gifts. Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, was her favourite at home but was suspected of murdering his wife and could never be openly courted. Last in line was Francis, Duke of Anjou, the French king’s brother, who came close to a deal in 1581.

Elizabeth said she preferred to remain the Virgin Queen. Each potential match brought drawbacks: a Catholic husband risked the religious settlement; a foreign prince risked drawing England into European wars; a domestic noble risked civil war between rival factions. Delay was, for Elizabeth, almost always safer than commitment. By the late 1570s she was past the typical age for childbirth, and by 1581 the marriage question was effectively closed.

Elizabeth used marriage negotiations as diplomacy. While Spain and France believed she might still wed their candidate, neither dared invade. Negotiations with the Duke of Anjou in 1581, for example, helped delay open war with Spain by several years. The image of an ‘available’ queen was politically useful even when the reality was that no marriage would happen. The historian Wallace MacCaffrey called this her ‘permanent ambiguity’.

The Succession Problem

No marriage meant no obvious heir. The senior Catholic claimant was Mary, Queen of Scots, the queen’s cousin. After Mary’s execution in 1587, the heir most ministers favoured was her Protestant son James VI of Scotland. Elizabeth refused to name him publicly. Naming an heir, she argued, would attract plotters — people would ‘set their eyes on the rising sun’. Yet the silence created the opposite anxiety: that her death might trigger civil war.

The risk grew through the 1590s. In 1595 the Catholic exile Robert Persons published a book arguing for the Spanish royal family’s right to the English throne. Robert Cecil therefore opened a secret correspondence with James VI, encouraging him to be patient and assuring him of support. When Elizabeth died on 24 March 1603, James was proclaimed king within hours. The succession was settled peacefully — but only because Cecil had quietly prepared the ground while the queen herself stayed silent.

The succession debate involves Mary, Queen of Scots — Elizabeth’s Catholic Stuart cousin who was held in England from 1568 and executed in 1587. She is not Mary I (Elizabeth’s Tudor half-sister), who died in 1558 before this depth study begins. Examiners flag this confusion every year as a top reason exam answers lose marks.

Key Fact

Elizabeth refused to name an heir to avoid creating a focus for plots. After Mary, Queen of Scots, was executed in 1587, Robert Cecil secretly prepared the way for Mary’s Protestant son, James VI of Scotland, who was proclaimed King James I within hours of Elizabeth’s death in March 1603.
before.exam_tip_html: For an ‘Explain Significance’ question on Elizabeth as a female ruler, show significance both at the time and over time. At the time: marriage negotiations were a diplomatic tool that delayed war with Spain. Over time: refusing to name James openly preserved her authority but transferred the risk to Robert Cecil to manage in secret.

practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It increased anxiety among ministers and gentry that Elizabeth’s death might trigger civil war between rival claimants.
• It encouraged Catholic writers abroad — for example Robert Persons in 1595 — to argue for foreign claims, including the Spanish royal family.
• It pushed Robert Cecil to open secret correspondence with James VI of Scotland from the late 1590s, ensuring a peaceful succession in 1603.
• It preserved Elizabeth’s personal authority by stopping ambitious nobles ‘setting their eyes on the rising sun’.

• Significance over time: clashes with Wentworth and others (1566, 1576) set early limits on royal control of debate that later parliaments would push back against.

lessons.title: Authority at the end of the reign and Essex's rebellion (1601)

before.content_html:
Authority Under Strain in the 1590s

By the 1590s Elizabeth was an old queen. She was 60 in 1593 and her ministers, courtiers and people knew she could not rule for much longer. The decade brought a run of crises: a long, expensive war with Spain after 1588; rebellion in Ireland led by the Earl of Tyrone; four bad harvests between 1594 and 1598 that pushed the price of grain above the reach of labourers; outbreaks of plague; and the deaths of Walsingham (1590) and Burghley (1598). Yet Elizabeth’s authority held, even as one of her own favourites — Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex — rose, fell and led a rebellion.

Why Authority Held

Elizabeth’s grip on power into the 1590s rested on five things. First, the patronage system — lands, monopolies, county offices — still flowed from her, so ambitious men competed for her favour. Second, the cult of Gloriana projected an unaging queen onto portraits and progresses, even as her health declined. Third, the long shadow of the 1588 Armada victory gave her credit she could draw on for years. Fourth, Robert Cecil quietly took on his father’s administrative weight after 1598. Fifth, the queen herself remained the source of final decisions; ministers competed for influence, but she chose between them.

Key Fact

Despite the war with Spain, Tyrone’s rebellion in Ireland, four bad harvests (1594–1598) and the deaths of Walsingham (1590) and Burghley (1598), Elizabeth kept her authority through patronage, the Gloriana image, the legacy of 1588, and Robert Cecil’s steady administration.

The Rise of Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex

Robert Devereux, 2nd Earl of Essex, was the stepson of Robert Dudley and Elizabeth’s closest court favourite from the late 1580s. He was charming, brave, well-educated and 33 years younger than the queen. He led English troops in France in 1591 and helped capture Cadiz from the Spanish in 1596. He cultivated a public image as a chivalrous war-leader at a time when the Cecil faction at court favoured negotiation. By the late 1590s he expected to inherit the senior offices that Burghley had held.

But Essex was rash. He quarrelled openly with the queen; on one famous occasion in 1598 he half-drew his sword at her in the Privy Chamber, an offence that another courtier would have died for. He treated the rivalry with Robert Cecil as a personal feud. He surrounded himself with discontented young nobles and military veterans — a pattern Walsingham’s old intelligence service watched closely.

Ireland and the Loss of Patronage

In 1599 Elizabeth sent Essex to Ireland with a large army to crush the rebellion of Hugh O’Neill, Earl of Tyrone. The campaign was a disaster. Essex avoided battle, made a private truce with Tyrone, and then abandoned his command and sailed home without permission. He burst, mud-stained, into the queen’s bedchamber at Nonsuch Palace in September 1599 — an unforgivable breach of royal protocol. He was placed under house arrest and forbidden the court.

The decisive blow came in 1600. Elizabeth refused to renew Essex’s monopoly on sweet wines, the income source on which his lavish household and political following depended. Without that patronage, his creditors closed in and his political support began to drain away. As we saw in earlier lessons, patronage was the glue that held the Elizabethan elite to the Crown. When Elizabeth withdrew it from a great noble whose followers had been promised offices and rewards, those followers had nowhere to go — except into rebellion.

A monopoly on sweet wines meant that Essex could charge a fee on every cask of imported sweet wine sold in England. The income paid for his household, his agents, his soldiers and his political dependents. When Elizabeth let the licence lapse in October 1600, his finances collapsed within months. Several historians, including Penry Williams, see this single decision as the trigger for the rebellion: Essex was not yet ruined, but he believed he soon would be.

Essex’s Rebellion, February 1601

On 8 February 1601, Essex marched out of his London home, Essex House on the Strand, with about 200–300 followers, mostly armed. His plan was to seize the queen, force her to dismiss Robert Cecil and pardon him. He hoped Londoners would join him as he walked through the city. They did not. The Privy Council acted fast: Cecil had been warned by informants and had already declared Essex a traitor. Royal heralds rode through the streets repeating the proclamation. By that afternoon Essex’s followers were melting away. He surrendered at Essex House by evening.

A trial followed at Westminster on 19 February. Essex was found guilty of treason. He was beheaded at the Tower on 25 February 1601, the last execution of an Elizabethan favourite. About five other ringleaders were also executed; the rest of the followers were fined or pardoned. Cecil, Essex’s rival, emerged unchallenged as the queen’s leading minister.

On 7 February 1601, the day before the rising, Essex’s supporters paid Shakespeare’s company, the Lord Chamberlain’s Men, to stage Richard II — a play that depicts the deposition of an unpopular monarch. They hoped it would prepare London opinion. The performance went ahead but failed in its political purpose; the company itself was investigated but cleared, on the grounds that they had simply taken paying customers. Elizabeth later remarked, ‘I am Richard II, know ye not that?’.

Key Fact

Essex’s rebellion failed within hours because Robert Cecil had been warned in advance, declared him a traitor, and got royal heralds onto the streets faster than Essex could rally support. Patronage withdrawn from one ambitious man could not be replaced overnight by armed force.
before.exam_tip_html: For an ‘Explain Significance’ question on Essex’s rebellion, give significance both at the time (the speed of its failure proved the strength of Cecil’s administration and intelligence) and over time (it confirmed that patronage, not military force, anchored Elizabethan rule, and cleared the way for Robert Cecil to manage the 1603 succession).

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the strength of Elizabeth’s authority in the 1590s.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Continued use of patronage — lands, monopolies and offices — to bind nobles to the Crown despite the deaths of Walsingham and Burghley.
• Active cultivation of the Gloriana image through portraits, court ceremony and progresses, even as the queen aged.

lessons.title: Religious matters: settlement, Catholics and Puritans

before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The 1559 Religious Settlement — the Acts of Supremacy and Uniformity — was a deliberate compromise: Protestant doctrine in a familiar Catholic-style service, with a 12-pence fine for non-attendance.
  • English Catholics divided into ‘Church Papists’ who outwardly conformed and recusants who refused; pressure on both grew sharply from 1581 onwards.
  • Puritans rejected the Settlement’s remaining Catholic features and were managed firmly — Grindal suspended in 1577, Whitgift enforcing the Three Articles after 1583, around 200 ministers deprived of their parishes.
before.content_html:
The Religious Inheritance of 1568

When this depth study opens in 1568, England’s religion had changed three times in a single generation. Henry VIII broke with Rome in the 1530s; Edward VI made the country firmly Protestant; Mary I restored Catholicism and burned around 280 Protestants. When Elizabeth came to the throne in 1558 she had to settle the question for a fourth time. The compromise she chose — the Religious Settlement of 1559 — would shape the next 35 years.

The Religious Settlement, 1559

The settlement was carried by two laws. The Act of Supremacy made Elizabeth ‘Supreme Governor’ of the Church of England (not ‘Supreme Head’, a title some thought wrong for a woman) and required clergy and officials to swear an oath of loyalty. The Act of Uniformity imposed a new English Book of Common Prayer on every parish, set out the form of services, and required attendance at Sunday worship. Those who failed to attend faced a fine of 12 pence.

The Settlement was deliberately a middle way. Doctrine was Protestant: the 39 Articles of 1563 affirmed salvation by faith and rejected the Catholic mass as a sacrifice. But the appearance of services kept some traditional Catholic features: priests wore vestments, churches kept altars, and the Prayer Book’s wording on communion was carefully ambiguous so that both Protestants and many Catholics could attend. Elizabeth’s aim was outward conformity — she famously said she had ‘no desire to make windows into men’s souls’.

Key Fact

The 1559 Religious Settlement was carried by two Acts: the Act of Supremacy (Elizabeth as Supreme Governor of the Church of England) and the Act of Uniformity (one English Prayer Book, compulsory Sunday attendance, 12-pence fine for staying away).

English Catholics

In 1568 a large minority of the population was still Catholic, especially in the north and west. Most attended Anglican services to avoid the fine and were nicknamed ‘Church Papists’. A smaller, more determined group refused to attend at all. They were called recusants — from the Latin ‘recusare’, ‘to refuse’.

Elizabeth and her ministers initially treated Catholics cautiously. The fines were enforced loosely; few priests were arrested in the 1560s; and the queen even tolerated private Catholic worship in some great households. Her concern was political loyalty, not theological purity. This relatively soft approach would harden sharply after 1569 (the Northern Rebellion) and 1570 (her excommunication) — the subject of the next lesson.

The Puritans

If Catholics found the Settlement too Protestant, the Puritans found it not Protestant enough. ‘Puritan’ was originally a term of insult for hardline Protestants who wanted to ‘purify’ the Church of remaining Catholic features. Their objections were specific: vestments looked too Catholic; the Prayer Book’s communion wording was too vague; bishops’ authority was too like the Roman hierarchy; church courts and saints’ days were superstition. Puritans wanted simpler services, more preaching, and church government by elected elders rather than bishops appointed by the Crown.

Puritans were not a single party. Many remained inside the Church of England and worked for reform from within — pressing through Parliament for changes to the Prayer Book. Others were Presbyterians, who wanted bishops abolished entirely. A small minority were Separatists, who left the Church to form independent congregations. Elizabeth saw the most radical Puritans as a political threat — their attacks on bishops, she argued, were attacks on her own authority over the Church.

In the 1560s some Puritan clergy refused to wear the surplice, the white robe required by the Prayer Book. Archbishop Parker, on Elizabeth’s orders, suspended around 37 London ministers in 1566. In the 1570s Puritans organised ‘prophesyings’ — meetings to discuss Bible passages and improve preaching. Archbishop Grindal refused to suppress them, arguing that better preaching was good for the Church. Elizabeth disagreed and suspended Grindal in 1577. After his death in 1583, John Whitgift was made archbishop with orders to enforce conformity strictly.

The Government’s Response, 1568–1603

Through the reign, the regime tightened the rules whenever a threat appeared. Recusancy fines rose sharply in 1581 (from 12 pence per Sunday to £20 per month). The 1585 Act made it treason to be a Catholic priest trained abroad and entering England; up to 130 priests were executed by 1603. From the 1580s, Whitgift’s ‘Three Articles’ required every clergyman to accept the queen’s supremacy, the Prayer Book and the 39 Articles. Roughly 200 Puritan ministers were deprived of their parishes for refusing.

For most ordinary parishioners, ‘outward conformity’ meant turning up at the parish church on a Sunday morning, listening to the Prayer Book service, and going home. It did not require enthusiasm. Many in the north of England, in country parishes far from London, kept old practices — saints’ days, holy wells, prayers for the dead — alongside attendance. The state was content with the appearance of compliance because punishing private belief was beyond its administrative reach.

Key Fact

Elizabeth aimed for outward conformity, not inner belief. The 1559 Settlement kept Catholic-style appearances (vestments, altars, ambiguous wording) but enforced Protestant doctrine through the Act of Supremacy and the 39 Articles. Both committed Catholics and hardline Puritans rejected the compromise; the rest were expected to attend church and keep their views private.

Avoid vague answers such as ‘people had to go to church’ without naming the law that made them.

lessons.title: The Northern Rebellion, excommunication and the missionary threat

before.content_html:
A Decade of Catholic Threat

The 1559 religious settlement had survived its first ten years, but in 1568 the situation changed sharply. Mary, Queen of Scots, fled into England after losing a Scottish civil war. As a Catholic with a strong claim to the English throne, she became an instant focus for any Catholic discontented with Elizabeth. Within twelve months, the country saw its largest rebellion of the reign; within fifteen months, the Pope declared Elizabeth no longer queen; within a decade, hundreds of trained Catholic missionaries were entering England in secret. This lesson follows that chain of events.

The Northern Rebellion, November 1569

The Northern Rebellion was led by two great northern earls: Thomas Percy, Earl of Northumberland, and Charles Neville, Earl of Westmorland. Their grievances were both religious and political. They were Catholics who resented the 1559 settlement; they had lost influence in the north as Elizabeth promoted southern Protestants; and they were drawn into a wider plan to marry Mary, Queen of Scots, to the Duke of Norfolk and force Elizabeth to recognise Mary as her heir. Norfolk was arrested before he could act.

On 14 November 1569 the earls and around 4,600 followers seized Durham Cathedral, tore up the English Prayer Book, and celebrated a Catholic mass for the first time in a decade. They marched south. But their numbers stalled below 6,000, the southern Catholics they hoped would rise stayed quiet, and a royal army under the Earl of Sussex moved north. By December the rebels had retreated; by January 1570 the earls had fled to Scotland; the rebellion was over. Around 450 rebels were hanged in their home villages on Elizabeth’s orders — a deliberately public punishment to deter further risings.

Key Fact

The Northern Rebellion of November 1569 was led by the Catholic earls of Northumberland and Westmorland. They seized Durham Cathedral, restored the Latin mass, and marched south — but failed to spread the rising. Around 450 rebels were hanged in their villages.

The Papal Excommunication, 1570

In February 1570, Pope Pius V issued the bull Regnans in Excelsis. He declared Elizabeth a heretic, excommunicated her, and released English Catholics from their oath of allegiance to the Crown. In effect, the Pope told Catholics they no longer had a religious duty to obey their queen — and that those who deposed or killed her would be acting in line with Catholic conscience.

The bull was a turning point. Before 1570, the regime could treat its Catholic subjects as politically loyal even if religiously different. After 1570 every recusant was, on paper, a potential traitor. The political consequence was almost immediate: a 1571 Treasons Act made it treason to import the bull or to call the queen a heretic, and recusancy fines began their long climb. The longer-term consequence was psychological: from 1570 the regime treated militant Catholicism as a national-security problem, not a pastoral one.

In May 1570, a London Catholic named John Felton nailed a copy of the papal bull to the gates of the Bishop of London’s palace. He was arrested, tortured, and executed in August. His action made the bull famous overnight. Felton’s defiance set the pattern for what missionary priests would later do: take a public stand for Catholic conscience and accept the consequences. He was canonised by Pope Paul VI in 1970.

The Missionary Priests

From the 1570s, English Catholics responded to the bull with a quiet counter-offensive. William Allen, an English Catholic in exile, opened a seminary at Douai (in modern Belgium) in 1568. Its purpose was to train English-speaking Catholic priests and send them home to keep Catholic worship alive. The first Douai priests reached England in 1574. Around 471 trained priests would enter England by the end of the reign. From 1580 the Jesuit Order joined the mission — the most famous arrivals being Edmund Campion and Robert Persons in June 1580.

The missionaries were not, in their own minds, plotters. Their task was sacramental: to hear confessions, say mass and baptise. But the regime saw them differently. After Regnans in Excelsis, any priest entering England in secret was assumed to be working for the queen’s deposition. The 1585 Act of Parliament made it treason for any Catholic priest trained abroad to be in England at all. Around 130 priests were executed during the reign, including Campion in 1581. Persons escaped to the Continent and went on writing in support of Catholic claims to the English throne.

The chain from 1569 to 1588 is unbroken. The Northern Rebellion fed Mary’s reputation as a Catholic figurehead. The 1570 bull made her a focus for plots, including Ridolfi (1571), Throckmorton (1583) and Babington (1586). Each plot tightened the laws against Catholics; tighter laws drove some English Catholics to Spain; Spanish willingness to invade was hardened by Mary’s execution in 1587. The Armada of 1588 is the last act of the same drama. Examiners reward answers that show this interaction, rather than treating each event in isolation.

The Threat in Context

It is easy to overstate the danger. The Northern Rebellion fizzled out within seven weeks; no English Catholic gentry of consequence joined the missionaries; ordinary Catholic parishioners mostly continued to attend church and pay their fines. But the regime felt the threat acutely. Walsingham’s intelligence service was built largely to track priests and plotters; the Privy Council’s correspondence in the 1580s is dominated by Catholic anxieties; and the increasingly harsh recusancy laws are unintelligible without 1569 and 1570 in the background.

Key Fact

The 1570 papal bull Regnans in Excelsis released English Catholics from loyalty to Elizabeth and was the moment the regime began to treat Catholicism as a national-security problem. The 1571 Treasons Act, the missionary priests, and the 1585 Act against them all flow directly from this turning point.
before.exam_tip_html: For an ‘Explain Significance’ question, treat 1569–1570 as a hinge. Significance at the time: a real armed rebellion, then a public papal endorsement of resistance, gave the regime urgent reasons to harden its policy. Significance over time: the laws and intelligence machinery built in response shaped every later Catholic crisis up to and including the Armada of 1588.

lessons.title: Mary, Queen of Scots: plots, trial and execution

before.content_html:
Mary’s Arrival in England, 1568

In May 1568, Mary, Queen of Scots, crossed the Solway Firth in a small fishing boat and threw herself on Elizabeth’s mercy. She was Elizabeth’s first cousin once removed, a Catholic, the great-granddaughter of Henry VII, and — for any English Catholic who rejected Henry VIII’s divorce — the rightful queen of England. She was also a fugitive: deposed by Scottish lords, suspected of involvement in the murder of her second husband, Lord Darnley, and forced to abdicate in favour of her infant son James. Elizabeth would not see her in person. Instead, Mary was placed under guard, first at Carlisle, then at a series of country houses in central England. She would remain a prisoner for the next nineteen years.

Key Fact

Mary, Queen of Scots, fled to England in May 1568 after losing a Scottish civil war. She was Elizabeth’s Catholic cousin and a rival claimant to the English throne. She was held under house arrest for 19 years, until her execution in February 1587.

Why Mary Was a Problem — Not Just a Prisoner

Killing Mary in 1568 was politically impossible. She was an anointed queen, a guest of the Crown, and a foreign sovereign. Releasing her was equally dangerous: she would head for France or Spain and become a Catholic figurehead abroad. So Elizabeth chose a third option — house arrest — and hoped the problem would solve itself. It did not. Mary was a magnet for every Catholic who hoped to undo the 1559 settlement. Within eighteen months her presence had helped trigger the Northern Rebellion of 1569, which aimed to free her and marry her to the Duke of Norfolk.

A common confusion at GCSE is between Mary, Queen of Scots, and Mary I — Elizabeth’s Tudor half-sister, who died in 1558 and never appears in this depth study. Mary Queen of Scots is the Stuart cousin, captured 1568, executed 1587. Keep them apart.

A Decade of Plots

Three major Catholic plots between 1571 and 1583 turned on Mary’s claim to the throne. The 1571 Ridolfi Plot proposed a Spanish invasion timed with an English Catholic rising; Norfolk was executed for treason in 1572, although Elizabeth spared Mary. The 1583 Throckmorton Plot proposed a French invasion led by Mary’s cousin the Duke of Guise; Walsingham’s agents discovered it and the Spanish ambassador was expelled. Each plot tightened the laws against Catholics and pushed Parliament to demand Mary’s execution. Each time, Elizabeth refused.

Elizabeth’s reluctance to execute Mary was not only personal. Killing an anointed queen would set a dangerous precedent for her own throne. It risked open war with Catholic France and Spain. It would damage her image as a merciful ruler. And it would martyr Mary — arguably making her more dangerous dead than alive. For nearly twenty years, Elizabeth chose the political risk of keeping Mary alive over the legal risk of killing her.

The Babington Plot, 1586

The third and decisive plot was led by Anthony Babington, a young Catholic gentleman, in the summer of 1586. The plan was to assassinate Elizabeth, free Mary, and place her on the throne with Spanish backing. The plotters wrote to Mary in cipher, smuggling letters in and out of her household at Chartley Hall hidden inside a beer barrel. What Babington did not know was that the brewer was working for Walsingham. Every letter was intercepted, copied, and read before being sent on. Walsingham’s code-breaker Thomas Phelippes deciphered them, including Mary’s reply approving the plot.

The trap closed in August 1586. Babington and his fellow conspirators were arrested, tried, and executed by hanging, drawing, and quartering in September. Mary was put on trial in October at Fotheringhay Castle. The court of nobles and judges found her guilty of complicity in plotting Elizabeth’s death.

Key Fact

The 1586 Babington Plot was uncovered when Walsingham’s agents intercepted ciphered letters smuggled in beer barrels at Chartley Hall. Mary’s written approval of Elizabeth’s assassination became the legal evidence that justified her trial and execution.

Execution at Fotheringhay, 8 February 1587

Parliament demanded Mary’s death; Elizabeth signed the death warrant in February 1587 but afterwards claimed she had not meant it to be carried out. Her secretary William Davison was sent to the Tower as a scapegoat. On 8 February 1587 Mary was beheaded in the great hall of Fotheringhay Castle. She wore a red petticoat — the colour of Catholic martyrdom — and forgave the executioner. The first axe blow missed her neck and struck her skull; it took three blows to kill her.

The execution shocked Catholic Europe. Philip II of Spain, who had until then preferred a Mary-led coup to a full invasion, now committed himself to launching the Armada the following year. Mary’s son James VI of Scotland, who would become James I of England in 1603, made a formal protest but accepted a pension and stayed quiet. Within England, the immediate effect was relief: the long source of Catholic plotting was gone.

Mary’s execution is the hinge between the religious crisis of the 1570s and the war crisis of 1588. Without her death, Philip II might have continued to wait. Without her death, the recusancy laws of the late 1580s would not have had Parliament’s full support. And without her death, the 1603 succession of her son James to the English throne — the Stuart line that would rule until 1714 — would have been politically impossible. Examiners reward students who follow these consequences across years rather than treating 1587 as an isolated event.

lessons.title: Conflict with Spain and the Spanish Armada (1588)

before.content_html:
From Cold War to Open War

By 1588 England and Spain had been drifting towards war for two decades. Three pressures converged. First, religion: Spain was the leading Catholic power in Europe, England was Protestant, and the Pope had excommunicated Elizabeth in 1570. Second, the Netherlands: when Dutch Protestants rebelled against Spanish rule in 1568, Elizabeth gave them quiet financial help, then in 1585 sent the Earl of Leicester with 6,000 English troops — an open act of war. Third, the sea: English ‘Sea Dogs’ like Drake and Hawkins had been raiding Spanish treasure ships in the Caribbean since the 1560s, and Drake’s circumnavigation (1577–1580) returned with around £400,000 in Spanish silver. The execution of Mary, Queen of Scots, in February 1587 was the final trigger; Philip II of Spain decided invasion was now the only answer.

Key Fact

The Spanish Armada of 1588 had three long-running causes — religion, the Dutch Revolt, and English raiding of Spanish treasure ships — and one trigger: the execution of Mary, Queen of Scots, in February 1587.

Philip’s Plan

Philip’s plan was an enterprise of England. The Armada — around 130 ships carrying 19,000 soldiers and 8,000 sailors — would sail from Lisbon up the English Channel, link with the Duke of Parma’s veteran army of 30,000 in the Spanish Netherlands, and ferry them across to land in Kent. London would fall, Elizabeth would be deposed, and a Catholic government installed. The plan depended on something Philip never quite secured: a deep-water port in the Netherlands where Parma’s flat-bottomed barges could meet the Armada in safety. Without that, the rendezvous would have to take place at sea — a far harder operation.

Drake delayed the launch by a year. In April 1587 he led a raid on Cadiz harbour, burning around 30 Spanish ships and destroying barrel staves needed to hold the Armada’s salt pork and water. Spanish supply, already strained, was set back by twelve months. Drake called it ‘singeing the King of Spain’s beard’.

English Naval Reform

By 1588 the English navy had been quietly transformed. Sir John Hawkins, as Treasurer of the Navy from 1577, had redesigned the fleet around race-built galleons: longer, narrower, lower in the water, faster, and carrying long-range bronze cannon along the side. Spanish ships, by contrast, were built for boarding: high-sided, packed with soldiers and short-range guns, designed to come alongside an enemy and fight hand to hand.

English crews trained to use this advantage at distance. Their tactic was to stand off, fire broadsides at long range, then turn away before the Spanish could close. The Spanish fleet, commanded by the inexperienced Duke of Medina Sidonia after the death of his predecessor, sailed in a tight crescent formation designed to keep the English boarders out — but unable to chase a faster enemy.

Lord Howard of Effingham was Lord High Admiral and overall commander — a Catholic from a noble family, chosen partly to reassure waverers. Sir Francis Drake was vice-admiral and the public face of the campaign. Sir John Hawkins commanded one of the four squadrons. Sir Martin Frobisher commanded another. None of them had fought a battle on this scale before, but together they represented the most experienced fighting sailors in Europe.

The Battle in the Channel, July 1588

The Armada was sighted off the Lizard on 19 July 1588. According to legend, Drake refused to leave his game of bowls at Plymouth Hoe, saying there was time to finish it and beat the Spaniards too. The story is probably fiction; the tide was wrong for sailing immediately. Over nine days the two fleets fought running battles up the Channel — off Eddystone, Portland Bill, and the Isle of Wight. Neither side scored a decisive blow. Spanish ships proved hard to sink with cannon fire alone; English supplies of powder and shot ran low.

On 27 July Medina Sidonia anchored at Calais, expecting Parma’s army to be ready. It was not — Parma had no deep-water port and his barges were still inland. The Armada was caught in an exposed roadstead with no rendezvous and no clear next move.

Fireships and Gravelines, 28–29 July

In the early hours of 28 July, the English sent eight fireships — old hulks packed with pitch and gunpowder, set alight and aimed at the Spanish anchorage. The Spanish cut their cables in panic to escape, breaking the crescent formation. The next morning, off the Flemish coast at Gravelines, the English fleet caught the scattered Spaniards in close action and pounded them at short range for nine hours. Several Spanish ships were sunk or captured; many more were damaged. The fleet was driven north into the North Sea.

Key Fact

The Armada was beaten by a combination of factors: English race-built ships and long-range cannon (technology), stand-off broadside tactics, the fireship attack at Calais and the failure of the Parma rendezvous (command), and the storms that wrecked many ships off Scotland and Ireland on the long voyage home (weather).

The Long Way Home

Unable to return down the Channel, Medina Sidonia took the surviving Armada north around Scotland and west of Ireland. Atlantic storms wrecked dozens of ships on the Irish coast; thousands of Spanish sailors and soldiers drowned or were killed by English forces ashore. Of the original 130 ships, only around 67 returned to Spain. Some 20,000 men were lost — most to disease and shipwreck, not battle. Elizabeth’s famous speech at Tilbury — ‘I have the heart and stomach of a king, and of a king of England too’ — was given on 9 August 1588 to the army assembled to repel an invasion that was already failing.

A common GCSE misconception is that the weather alone defeated the Armada — the so-called ‘Protestant Wind’. Weather mattered greatly on the voyage home, but the Armada had already lost its strategic purpose at Calais on 28 July, before the worst storms began. The fireships, the failure of the Parma rendezvous, and English ship design were what broke the formation. The storms then finished the job. Examiners reward students who weigh all four factors rather than collapsing the answer into ‘the weather’.

Avoid the trap of writing the story of the battle — the question is about effects, not narrative.

lessons.title: Living standards, fashion and the rise of the gentry

before.content_html:
A ‘Golden Age’ for Whom?

The phrase Golden Age was not invented by Elizabethans. It was attached to the late Tudor period by later writers who admired its theatre, exploration and architecture. For some people in the 1570s and 1580s the label fits well. The middling sort — landowners, merchants, lawyers, prosperous farmers — saw a real rise in living standards. They built bigger houses, bought more clothes, ate more meat, and read more books. Yet for the labouring poor the same decades brought rising prices, harvest failures, and harsher Poor Laws. The same period that produced Shakespeare also produced the 1572 statute classifying jobless beggars as criminals. A useful working answer is “Golden Age for some, harder times for others” — not the soft ‘everyone benefited’ story.

Key Fact

The ‘Golden Age’ label was applied to Elizabethan England by later writers and reflects only part of the picture — the lives of the gentry and middling sort. The same decades brought a sharp rise in vagrancy, harsher recusancy laws, and harvest failures for the poor.

The Rise of the Gentry

The biggest social change of the period was the rise of the gentry. They sat below the great nobility but above ordinary farmers and town tradesmen. Three things expanded their wealth and power. First, the dissolution of the monasteries under Henry VIII (1536–40) had thrown vast amounts of church land onto the market; gentry families bought it cheap and farmed it for profit. Second, rising food prices in the 1570s and 1580s meant that those who owned land made more money — the same harvest, sold at higher prices. Third, Elizabeth deliberately drew the gentry into local government: most justices of the peace, sheriffs, militia captains, and members of Parliament were gentry. By 1600 they ran county England.

Their growing confidence shows in their houses. The Elizabethan style favoured tall windows of small leaded panes, decorative chimneys, and ground-plans shaped like the letter E or H — a play on Elizabeth’s own name. Hardwick Hall in Derbyshire, built for Bess of Hardwick from 1590, was famous for having “more glass than wall”. Glass was expensive; using it on this scale was a public statement of wealth and loyalty to the queen.

Historians sometimes call the period 1570–1640 the Great Rebuilding because so many gentry, yeomen and prosperous craftsmen replaced timber and wattle houses with brick or stone, added a second floor, and put glass in the windows. Houses gained separate bedrooms, fireplaces in private rooms, and proper chimneys instead of central hearths. Better housing reflected real gains in middling-sort wealth — but the labouring poor lived in cottages little changed from the medieval period.

Living Standards: What Improved

For those above the labouring poor, daily life became more comfortable across Elizabeth’s reign. Diet improved: meat, dairy and white wheat bread replaced the rye and pottage of poorer households. Pewter replaced wood for tableware in middle-class homes; chairs replaced benches; mattresses stuffed with feathers replaced straw. Demand for new goods grew — books, clocks, mirrors, sugar, tobacco, and increasingly tea and spices brought in by long-distance merchants. The rise of the print trade in London put cheap pamphlets, almanacs and Bibles within reach of literate households for the first time.

Fashion and the Sumptuary Laws

Elizabethan fashion was loud and political. Wealthy men wore doublets, padded breeches, and starched white ruffs that grew comically large by the 1580s. Wealthy women wore farthingales (hooped skirts), tight bodices, and elaborate sleeves. Colour mattered: rich purple, deep red, black with silver, pearls and embroidery were status symbols. Elizabeth’s own image was a careful performance — the white face paint, jewelled gowns, and the unmarried ‘Virgin Queen’ persona were political tools, not personal vanity.

The regime tried to control all this through sumptuary laws — rules about which colours and fabrics each social rank could wear. A 1574 statute, for example, restricted purple silk and cloth-of-gold to the royal family and the highest nobility. The laws are revealing because they barely worked: the very fact that gentry and merchants kept dressing above their rank shows how blurred the social hierarchy was becoming.

Key Fact

Sumptuary laws (such as the 1574 statute) restricted which colours and fabrics each social rank could wear. Their repeated reissue and weak enforcement show that gentry and merchants were increasingly dressing above their rank — evidence the social hierarchy was loosening, not tightening.

Limits of the Boom

It is important not to mistake the gentry’s gains for general prosperity. The rising food prices that enriched landowners squeezed labourers; harvest failures in 1586, 1594 and 1596–97 caused real hunger; wages did not keep pace with prices for the unskilled. The growth of London (around 50,000 in 1500, perhaps 200,000 by 1600) brought wealth and culture but also overcrowded slums, plague, and the new visible poverty that scared the regime into the Poor Laws of 1572, 1576 and 1598. The Golden Age and the Poor Law era are the same period.

The 16-mark essay often invites students to weigh “how far” Elizabethan England was a Golden Age. Top-band answers do not just list achievements (theatre, exploration, the Armada). They balance the gentry’s rise and middling-sort prosperity against the poverty, harvest failures, and persecution that ran in parallel. The fact that the same decade gave us the rise of the gentry and the 1572 Vagabonds Act is the heart of a strong answer.

For an ‘Explain Effects’ question on the rise of the gentry, link wealth to political power: more gentry as JPs, sheriffs and MPs reshaped county government and Parliament.

• The wider European context made even modest English stability look golden by comparison.

lessons.title: Poverty, vagrancy and the Elizabethan Poor Laws

before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Elizabethan poverty rose sharply because of population growth (3 to 4 million by 1601), inflation, enclosure for sheep farming, and harvest failures — especially in 1586, 1594 and 1596–97.
  • Elizabethans split the poor into the impotent (deserving) and the sturdy beggars (undeserving); fear of disorder, not just charity, drove the government to act.
  • The 1572, 1576 and 1598 Poor Laws made the parish the basic unit of welfare, funded by a compulsory poor rate and run by elected Overseers; the system lasted until the New Poor Law of 1834.
before.content_html:
A Sharp Rise in Visible Poverty

Poverty was not new in 1568, but its scale and visibility changed dramatically across Elizabeth’s reign. Contemporaries reported large bands of jobless men and women on the roads, swelling crowds of beggars in market towns, and overcrowded slums in London. Modern historians estimate that perhaps half of England’s population lived close to the poverty line by 1600, with around a quarter falling below it in years of crisis. The Elizabethan poor were not a single group: they ranged from elderly widows unable to work, to skilled craftsmen squeezed by inflation, to the so-called sturdy beggars — able-bodied wanderers feared as criminals.

Key Fact

Elizabethan poverty had four main drivers: a population rise from around 3 million in 1551 to around 4 million by 1601, sharp inflation in food prices, the enclosure of common land for sheep farming, and bad harvests — especially the crisis years of 1586, 1594 and 1596–97.

Causes of the Increase

Population growth was the deepest cause. England’s population grew by roughly a third between 1551 and 1601 — from around 3 million to around 4 million — outpacing food production. More mouths chasing the same harvests pushed prices up. Wages did not keep pace: a craftsman’s real wage in 1600 was substantially lower than in 1500. Enclosure made things worse for many. Landowners fenced off common fields for sheep, evicting tenants and removing the grazing and gleaning rights that had cushioned poor families. Sheep farming needed fewer workers than arable farming, so jobs disappeared.

Bad harvests were the trigger. The 1586 harvest failed; 1594, 1595 and 1596 produced what contemporaries called “the four wet years”; 1596–97 saw genuine famine in parts of the north and Cumbria. The cloth trade, which employed thousands in East Anglia and the West Country, suffered repeated slumps. The dissolution of the monasteries decades earlier had also removed the largest single source of charity for the rural poor — abbeys had run almshouses and food doles that no longer existed by Elizabeth’s reign.

From the 1580s the war with Spain in the Netherlands and Ireland sent thousands of English soldiers and sailors back to England with no land, no wages, and often serious wounds. Veterans of the Armada campaign were paid late or not at all and many turned to begging. They are part of the reason the 1593 statute distinguished ‘maimed soldiers’ as a deserving category, separate from sturdy beggars.

Attitudes to the Poor

Elizabethans drew a hard line between two kinds of poor: the impotent poor — the elderly, disabled, orphaned, sick, who could not work — and the able-bodied poor, expected to work or be punished. The impotent poor were treated with sympathy and given parish relief. The able-bodied jobless were treated with suspicion: many people genuinely believed sturdy beggars were lazy criminals, that begging spread plague, and that wandering bands threatened public order. Religious thinking made this worse: Calvinist Protestants tended to see worldly success as a sign of God’s favour and poverty as a sign of moral failure.

The fear of disorder mattered more than charity in driving government action. The Privy Council’s correspondence in the 1580s and 1590s is full of warnings of riots in market towns when grain prices spiked. The Oxfordshire Rising of 1596 — a small attempted uprising by a few dozen poor men — was a real warning of what hunger might unleash.

The Poor Laws of 1572, 1576 and 1598

Parliament responded with three major statutes. The 1572 Vagabonds Act, the harshest, classified jobless beggars as criminals: a first offence brought whipping and ear boring; a second made them felons; a third meant the death penalty. But the same act introduced the first compulsory poor rate — a property tax raised parish by parish to support the deserving poor. The 1576 Poor Relief Act required every town to provide raw materials (wool, flax, hemp) so that the able-bodied could be put to work, and to set up a House of Correction for those who refused. The 1598 Act for the Relief of the Poor, consolidated into the famous 1601 Poor Law, made the parish the basic unit of welfare for over two centuries afterwards. Each parish elected unpaid Overseers of the Poor to collect the poor rate and distribute relief.

Key Fact

The Elizabethan Poor Laws of 1572, 1576 and 1598 split the poor into deserving (impotent) and undeserving (sturdy beggars), funded relief through a compulsory parish poor rate, set the able-bodied to work, and made the parish — not central government — the unit of welfare for the next 250 years.

How the System Worked in Practice

The 1598 system rested on the parish. Each year, parishioners elected two Overseers of the Poor from the better-off householders. The overseers collected the poor rate, paid pensions to the elderly and disabled, found apprenticeships for poor children, and bought materials for the workhouse. Vagrants caught wandering were whipped and sent back to their parish of birth or last legal settlement — the principle that one’s home parish was responsible for one’s welfare. The London authorities went further with their own institutions: Bridewell handled idle vagrants, Bethlem the mentally ill, and Christ’s Hospital orphaned children.

Strengths: the Poor Laws were the first nationally organised system of welfare in Europe; they channelled local charitable energy through the parish; they survived virtually unchanged until 1834. Weaknesses: relief depended on the willingness of parishes to tax themselves — some did, others did not. The harsh treatment of vagrants did little to address root causes. And the deserving/undeserving distinction obscured the fact that most able-bodied poor were jobless because there was no work, not because they refused to take it. Examiners reward students who weigh both sides.

For an ‘Explain Effects’ question, focus on named consequences: the compulsory poor rate, the role of Overseers of the Poor, and the legal split between deserving and undeserving poor.

lessons.title: English sailors: Hawkins, Drake, Raleigh and exploration

before.content_html:
Why Elizabethans Took to the Sea

By the 1560s, Spain and Portugal already controlled most known sea routes to the Americas, Africa and Asia, and treated those routes as their private property. England was a small, second-rank naval power that wanted in. Three things drove Elizabethan sailors to push past Spanish and Portuguese monopolies: the lure of profit from gold, silver and spices; the religious rivalry that made attacking Catholic Spain seem patriotic; and Elizabeth’s willingness to license private captains to do what her navy could not officially do. The most famous of these captains were John Hawkins, Francis Drake and Walter Raleigh — all West Country gentlemen, all closely connected to the court.

Key Fact

Hawkins ran the first English slaving voyages in the 1560s and later redesigned the navy. Drake circumnavigated the globe between 1577 and 1580 and was knighted by Elizabeth on board his ship. Raleigh launched the failed Roanoke colony in 1585–87, England’s first attempt at settling North America.

John Hawkins and the First Slaving Voyages

John Hawkins made three slave-trading voyages between 1562 and 1568. He sailed to West Africa, where he seized or bought captive Africans, then crossed the Atlantic to sell them to Spanish colonists in the Caribbean in exchange for sugar, hides and pearls. Hawkins’s voyages broke the Spanish trade monopoly and made him — and his investors, including Elizabeth herself — a large profit. The third voyage ended in disaster at San Juan de Ulua in 1568 when a Spanish fleet ambushed Hawkins’s ships, killing most of his men. The young Francis Drake was on the voyage and barely escaped. He never forgave Spain.

Hawkins’s most lasting contribution was not the slaving but what he did afterwards. From 1577, as Treasurer of the Navy, he redesigned English warships into the lighter, faster, more heavily gunned vessels known as ‘race-built’ galleons. These were the ships that would defeat the Armada eleven years later. The slaving voyages themselves are a moral stain on the period: Hawkins’s coat of arms, granted by Elizabeth, openly featured a bound African captive.

Hawkins’s three voyages trafficked an estimated 1,200–1,400 Africans across the Atlantic. This was tiny compared with the later British slave trade of the 1700s, which trafficked millions, but it set a legal and commercial precedent: an English crew, with royal investment, treating human beings as cargo. After Hawkins, English slaving paused for about a century — until renewed and industrialised after 1660 — but the Elizabethan voyages are the start of that history, and modern historians and museums increasingly stress this part of the ‘Golden Age’ story.

Francis Drake’s Circumnavigation, 1577–1580

In December 1577 Drake left Plymouth with five ships on a secret royal commission to raid Spanish ports along the Pacific coast of South America. By the time he returned to Plymouth in September 1580 he had sailed all the way around the world — only the second commander in history to do so, after the Portuguese-Spanish expedition of Magellan-Elcano in 1522. Drake had passed through the storms of the Strait of Magellan, raided the unprotected Spanish ports of Valparaiso and Callao, captured the treasure ship Nuestra Senora de la Concepcion (nicknamed the Cacafuego), claimed the coast of California for Elizabeth as ‘New Albion’, and sailed home across the Pacific and Indian Oceans.

The financial return was extraordinary. Drake brought back gold, silver and jewels worth perhaps £400,000 — more than a year of normal Crown income. Investors received roughly £47 for every £1 they had risked, and Elizabeth’s personal share allowed her to clear most of her foreign debts. In April 1581 she came on board Drake’s ship the Golden Hind at Deptford and knighted him on deck. Spain was furious: Philip II called Drake ‘El Draque’ (‘the Dragon’) and demanded his execution. Elizabeth refused.

Key Fact

Drake’s circumnavigation lasted from December 1577 to September 1580. It made England the second nation to sail around the globe, brought back roughly £400,000 in plunder, struck a propaganda blow against Spain, and provided a model for later English voyages of trade and exploration.

Walter Raleigh and the Roanoke Colony

Walter Raleigh was a court favourite of Elizabeth in the 1580s — soldier, poet, courtier, and from 1585 the holder of a royal patent to plant an English colony in North America. He never sailed to Roanoke himself but bankrolled and organised the expeditions. The first attempt, in 1585, landed about 100 men on Roanoke Island off the coast of modern North Carolina. Short of food and clashing with the local Algonquian inhabitants, the colonists abandoned the site after a year and sailed home with Drake when he stopped by on his way back from raiding the Caribbean.

A second colony was planted in 1587 under Governor John White and included around 115 men, women and children — among them White’s daughter Eleanor Dare, who gave birth to Virginia Dare, the first English child born in the Americas. White returned to England for supplies, but the war with Spain meant no relief ship reached Roanoke until 1590. By then the colony had vanished. The only clue was the word ‘CROATOAN’ carved on a post. The fate of the Roanoke colonists has never been confirmed.

Roanoke failed for several connected reasons. The site was poorly chosen: shallow inlets made it hard to resupply by sea. The colonists arrived too late in the season to plant crops and quickly became dependent on the Algonquian for food, which broke down into violence. Raleigh’s organisation underfunded the venture, and the war with Spain pulled every available ship into home defence after 1588. England would not successfully plant a North American colony until Jamestown in 1607 — a generation later. Raleigh himself fell from royal favour in 1592, was imprisoned by James I in 1603, and was eventually executed in 1618.

The Bigger Picture: Voyages, Trade and Profit

Behind the famous names, Elizabethan sea power had a wider dimension. The Muscovy Company (1555) traded with Russia. The Levant Company (1581) opened trade with the Ottoman Empire. The East India Company, founded just before the end of the reign in 1600, would eventually overshadow them all. Privateering — legalised piracy under royal licence — brought thousands of Spanish prizes home to West Country ports. The Sea Dogs, as Drake’s circle were known, were both heroes of national propaganda and pirates by Spanish definition. By 1603 England was not yet an imperial power, but the institutional and commercial base for empire was visibly being assembled.

For a ‘Describe Two Features’ question on the voyages or Roanoke, give two distinct features with one supporting detail each — do not write a paragraph.
