lessons.title: The Elizabethan theatre and attitudes towards it

before.content_html:
A New Kind of Entertainment

Before Elizabeth’s reign, plays in England had mostly been performed by travelling troupes in inn yards, in the halls of great houses, or as religious pageants run by town guilds. By 1600 something very different was happening: purpose-built playhouses outside the city walls of London were drawing audiences of two or three thousand people, several afternoons a week, paying a penny each. The Elizabethan public theatre was new in scale, in business model and in cultural reach. It was also a flashpoint — loved at court, distrusted by the City of London authorities, and attacked outright by Puritan critics.

Key Fact

Elizabethan theatre boomed because of three connected factors: noble patronage that protected actors from vagrancy laws, the rise of a paying urban audience with disposable income, and Elizabeth’s personal taste for plays at court. The first purpose-built public playhouse, The Theatre, opened in 1576 in Shoreditch.

Patronage and the Companies

Acting was not legally a respectable profession. The 1572 Vagabonds Act listed unattached actors alongside sturdy beggars and threatened them with whipping unless they had a noble patron. The result was that every successful Elizabethan acting company was named after a great lord. The Lord Chamberlain’s Men — led by Richard Burbage, with William Shakespeare as a sharer — were patronised by the Lord Chamberlain at court. The Admiral’s Men, who performed at the Rose, were patronised by the Lord Admiral. Patronage gave companies legal cover, social respectability and access to court performances.

The companies themselves were small. A typical company had around twelve sharers (men who owned a stake in the business), a few hired men for smaller parts, and four or five boy apprentices who played all the female roles — women were not allowed on the public stage. Plays were performed in repertory: a different play each afternoon, six days a week, with new plays added constantly. Playwrights such as Shakespeare, Christopher Marlowe and Ben Jonson wrote at speed for these companies.

Playhouses were polygonal wooden buildings, open to the sky in the middle, around three storeys high. Audiences stood in the central yard for one penny — these were the groundlings — or paid two pennies for a seat in the covered galleries, with cushions an extra penny on top. Performances ran in the afternoon because there was no artificial lighting. Special effects were limited but inventive: cannon fire, trapdoors, suspended thrones lowered from the ‘heavens’ above the stage, and pig’s blood for stabbings.

An Audience of Everyone

The most striking thing about an Elizabethan playhouse audience was its mix. Apprentices, dock workers and prostitutes rubbed shoulders with merchants, country gentry visiting London, courtiers and foreign visitors. The Spanish ambassador watched alongside soldiers and sailors. A penny was within reach of even a working Londoner: one Tudor commentator complained that apprentices were skipping work to stand at plays. This breadth of audience is one reason Shakespeare’s plays move between high poetry, sword fights, jokes about bodily functions and royal politics within a single scene — he was writing for a paying public that contained every social rank.

The cultural ambition of the plays grew quickly. Christopher Marlowe’s Doctor Faustus (c.1592) and Tamburlaine (1587) brought blank verse and big philosophical themes to a popular audience. Shakespeare’s histories — Henry V (1599), the Henry VI trilogy, Richard III — turned recent English politics into a public conversation. By 1600, Elizabethan playwrights were producing work that historians of literature treat as the foundation of modern English drama.

Opposition: City of London and the Puritans

Not everyone approved. The City of London Corporation — the merchant council that ran the City inside its medieval walls — banned public playhouses from operating on its territory from 1574. The Corporation gave four reasons: playhouses spread plague by drawing crowds; they attracted pickpockets, prostitutes and brawlers; they pulled apprentices away from honest work; and they encouraged immorality. This is why almost every Elizabethan playhouse stood just outside the City’s jurisdiction — in Shoreditch to the north (The Theatre, the Curtain), or south of the river in Southwark (the Rose, the Swan), where the Corporation’s writ did not run.

Puritan critics went further. Puritans argued that the theatre was sinful in itself — it taught vanity, glorified violence, mixed the sexes (boys playing women), and tempted people from honest work and worship. The Puritan minister Philip Stubbes’s Anatomy of Abuses (1583) attacked plays as ‘the schools of vice’ and called for them to be shut. London preachers blamed plague outbreaks on God’s anger at the playhouses. During serious plague, the Privy Council itself ordered playhouses closed — in 1592–94, in 1603 and several times after — partly to control infection, partly to placate the City and the Puritans. When the Puritans came to power in the 1640s they would close the theatres entirely, for eighteen years.

Key Fact

Opposition to the theatre came from two main directions. The City of London Corporation banned playhouses from 1574 because they spread plague, drew pickpockets and pulled apprentices from work. Puritans went further and called the theatre sinful in itself. This is why playhouses were built in Shoreditch and Southwark, outside the City’s jurisdiction.

Theatre and the Court

Against this opposition the theatre had a powerful protector: Elizabeth herself. The Queen’s Men was an acting company set up in 1583 specifically to perform for her at court, and the Lord Chamberlain’s Men performed at Whitehall and Greenwich during the winter season. Court patronage gave the theatre a status the Puritan press could not undo while the Queen lived.

A 1581 royal proclamation set up the Master of the Revels to license plays before performance — a system that protected the companies as much as it censored them, since a licensed play could not be banned by the City of London Corporation. The boom of the 1590s — the decade of Romeo and Juliet and Henry V, when several new playhouses were built south of the Thames — happened with the Queen’s active blessing.

For an ‘Explain Effects’ question on attitudes to theatre, focus on consequences: where playhouses were built (Shoreditch, Southwark), the Privy Council closures during plague, and the Puritan groundwork for the 1642 closures.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of an Elizabethan public playhouse.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Open-air structure: playhouses were polygonal wooden buildings, around three storeys high, with a central yard open to the sky and covered galleries around the sides.
• Mixed audience pricing: groundlings paid one penny to stand in the yard, two pennies bought a gallery seat, and a cushion cost one penny extra.
• Performance times: plays were performed in the afternoon because there was no artificial lighting strong enough for evening performances.
• Boy actors: women were not allowed on the public stage, so boy apprentices played all female roles in companies like the Lord Chamberlain’s Men.

Mastering: Two genuinely distinct features, each with one supporting detail.
Secure: Two features with limited supporting detail.
Developing: Two features identified but only described briefly.
Emerging: One feature, or two features without detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of noble patronage on the Elizabethan theatre.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Legal cover: the 1572 Vagabonds Act classed unattached actors as vagrants, but actors with a noble patron were exempt — patronage was the difference between a respectable career and being whipped.
• Stable companies: companies named after their patron (Lord Chamberlain’s Men, Lord Admiral’s Men, the Queen’s Men from 1583) developed long-term casts and shared business stakes among their sharers.
• Court access: patronage opened the door to court performances at Whitehall and Greenwich, which paid more than public performances and reinforced the company’s status.
• Protection from the City: a play licensed by the Master of the Revels under noble patronage could not easily be banned by the City of London Corporation.

Mastering: Multiple effects developed with named patrons, dates and outcomes.
Secure: Two or more effects clearly explained.
Developing: Effects identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Simple statements without development.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Puritan opposition to the Elizabethan theatre.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: • Moral attack on plays: Puritan writers such as Philip Stubbes in Anatomy of Abuses (1583) called the playhouses ‘schools of vice’ that taught vanity, violence and idleness. • Objection to boys playing women: Puritans argued that boys dressing as women on stage was scandalous and broke biblical commandments. • Plague theology: London Puritan preachers argued that plague outbreaks were God’s judgement on the playhouses and demanded their closure. • Long-term goal: Puritans pushed for outright abolition of the theatre — which they achieved in 1642 once Parliament took power, closing the theatres for eighteen years. Mastering: Two genuinely distinct features, each with one supporting detail. Secure: Two features with limited supporting detail. Developing: Two features identified but only described briefly. Emerging: One feature, or two features without detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of City of London opposition on where Elizabethan playhouses were built.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The City of London Corporation banned playhouses from operating inside the City walls from 1574, citing plague, crime and disorder.
• As a direct effect, purpose-built playhouses such as The Theatre (1576) and the Curtain were built in Shoreditch, just north of the City limits.
• The Rose and the Swan were built in Southwark, on the south bank of the Thames, outside the City’s jurisdiction; further playhouses followed there in the late 1590s.
• The result was a permanent geography of theatre on the edges of the City — clustered with bear-baiting rings, taverns and brothels — that defined Elizabethan and Jacobean playgoing.

Mastering: Multiple effects developed with named playhouses and dates.
Secure: Two or more effects clearly explained.
Developing: Effects identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Simple statements without development.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of an Elizabethan acting company in the 1590s.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Sharer system: the Lord Chamberlain’s Men was made up of around a dozen sharers who jointly owned the business; Shakespeare and Richard Burbage were both sharers.
• Boy apprentices: female roles were performed by boy apprentices, since women were not allowed on the public stage.
• Repertory performance: companies performed a different play each afternoon, six days a week, with new plays added constantly.
• Noble patron: every successful company was legally tied to a patron (the Lord Chamberlain, the Lord Admiral, the Queen herself), which protected the actors from the 1572 Vagabonds Act.

Mastering: Two genuinely distinct features, each with one supporting detail.
Secure: Two features with limited supporting detail.
Developing: Two features identified but only described briefly.
Emerging: One feature, or two features without detail.

practice_questions.text: Argue, using evidence from across the reign, that the Elizabethan theatre survived because of royal protection more than because of public popularity.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include arguments in support (royal protection mattered most):
• The 1572 Vagabonds Act would have shut down acting altogether if the Crown had not allowed noble patrons to exempt their companies.
• Elizabeth set up the Queen’s Men in 1583 specifically to perform at court, signalling royal endorsement.
• The Master of the Revels system from 1581 licensed plays under royal authority, blocking the City of London from banning licensed work.
• When the Puritans took political power in 1642, public popularity was no protection — the theatres were closed for eighteen years, showing royal backing was the missing ingredient.

Arguments to weigh against (public popularity mattered most):
• A penny entry brought audiences of two to three thousand several afternoons a week — the business model was self-sustaining.
• The geographic spread of playhouses (The Theatre 1576, the Curtain, the Rose, the Swan, and further Southwark playhouses by the late 1590s) shows commercial demand drove construction, not court order.
• The mixed audience — apprentices, gentry, courtiers, foreigners — meant the theatre had a constituency the Crown could not have manufactured.
• Playwrights like Marlowe and Shakespeare wrote in part for a paying public and shaped their work to it; the cultural achievement is not a court-only product.

A strong response weighs the role of royal patronage and licensing against the commercial vitality of the public playhouses, and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Mastering: Sustained argument with embedded evidence and a justified judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence on both sides.
Developing: Some argument; evidence may be limited.
Emerging: Simple points; little argument or judgement.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Calais anchorage as a site in the Armada campaign.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It was an open roadstead rather than an enclosed harbour, leaving the fleet exposed to weather and to attack from windward — the Armada anchored there only because no deep-water port was available.
• Ships lay at anchor packed closely together, which is what made the fireship attack on the night of 28 July so effective.
• Escape required cutting anchor cables, so the fleet left its best anchors on the seabed — with fatal consequences on the storm coasts of the route home.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the English fleet that faced the Armada in 1588.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Race-built galleons — longer, lower and faster than the Spanish ships, designed for gunnery rather than boarding.
• Long-range culverins, allowing the English to bombard from distances at which Spanish soldiers could not grapple and board.
• Home ports along the Channel (Plymouth and the anchorages up-Channel), giving resupply of powder, shot and food that the Armada, far from any friendly harbour, could not match.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Spain's lack of a deep-water port for the outcome of the Armada campaign.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It broke the rendezvous: the Armada could not wait safely anywhere near Parma's army, while Dunkirk and Nieuwpoort were too shallow for the galleons and blockaded by Dutch flyboats.
• It forced the fleet into the exposed Calais roadstead — the precondition for the fireship attack that broke the crescent without a battle.
• It denied repair and resupply: every English ship fought a day's sail from a friendly port; the Armada fought at the end of a supply line stretching to Spain.
• Ultimately it made the whole plan depend on perfect timing between a fleet and an army that could not communicate — a flaw visible on the map before a shot was fired.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the fireship attack at Calais changed the course of the Armada campaign.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The situation on 27 July: the Armada anchored in the open roadstead, ammunition low, Parma needing days he did not have, the English fleet anchored to windward.
• The attack: eight fireships, loaded with pitch and powder, sent down the wind in darkness into the packed anchorage.
• The immediate result: captains cut their cables; the crescent formation that a week of gunnery had failed to break was scattered in one night.
• The consequences: the scattered fleet was caught at Gravelines short of shot; the abandoned anchors doomed ships on the storm coasts of the north-about route home.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the weather in the defeat of the Spanish Armada.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The weather gauge: holding the upwind position let the English choose the range and timing of every engagement in the Channel.
• The double shift after Gravelines: wind first drove the Armada towards the Zeeland sandbanks, then backed just in time to spare it — but pushed it into the North Sea, making the north-about route the only way home.
• The autumn gales: storms on the Scottish and Irish coasts destroyed more ships than English gunfire, finishing a fleet that could no longer anchor.
• Balance: weather alone does not explain the defeat — the plan's geographical flaw and English gunnery created the situation the storms completed; 'God blew and they were scattered' was propaganda as well as piety.

practice_questions.text: 'The Spanish Armada was defeated by geography rather than by the English navy.' How far does a study of the Armada campaign support this statement? Explain your answer. You should refer to the campaign and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Support for the statement (site evidence):
• The missing deep-water port made the rendezvous with Parma close to impossible before the fleets ever met.
• The Calais roadstead's exposure enabled the fireships; the Zeeland banks nearly wrecked the fleet; the north-about route and Atlantic storms destroyed perhaps half of it — far more than battle did.
Against the statement (site evidence and context):
• English choices exploited the geography: refusing to board, holding the weather gauge, striking with fireships at the one moment the anchorage made them decisive.
• Race-built ships and culverins won Gravelines on gunnery, breaking ships and morale before the storms took over.
• The Dutch flyboat blockade — allied action, not geography — pinned Parma in port.
A developed judgement weighing environmental causes against human agency is required for the top level.

before.content_html:
A Castle Rebuilt Around One Guest

Kenilworth Castle is your specified site for the 2028 exam. It is a medieval fortress in Warwickshire — Norman keep, great mere, John of Gaunt’s hall — but the exam is not really about the Middle Ages. It is about what Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, did to the place in the 1570s, and above all about nineteen days in July 1575 when he staged the most lavish entertainment of the reign for Elizabeth I. Read the site properly and it opens up half your course: the court, royal progresses, the marriage question, and the politics of spending money to be loved.

Dudley and the Gift of a Castle

Kenilworth came to Dudley from the queen herself: she granted him the castle in 1563, the year before she made him Earl of Leicester. He was her favourite — the man she called her ‘eyes’, master of the horse, privy councillor, and for decades the most plausible husband she never took (Lesson 3). The gift was typical of how Elizabeth ruled her court: favour made visible in land and stone. What Dudley then spent on the place turned a royal gift into a royal argument — a castle rebuilt as a machine for entertaining one woman.

Key Fact

Elizabeth granted Kenilworth to Robert Dudley in 1563. For her visits he added a four-storey tower of state apartments — Leicester’s Building — raised a grand new gatehouse, modernised the medieval keep with great windows, and laid out a privy garden fit for a queen.

Reading the Site: What Leicester Built

The additions are still legible in the ruins, and each one is evidence. Leicester’s Building was a slender four-storey block of glittering state apartments, built so the queen and her ladies could lodge in modern comfort beside the medieval great hall — a private palace bolted onto a fortress. The gatehouse gave arriving courtiers a fashionable first impression (and survives intact, because later owners made it a house). The Norman keep was kept — twelfth-century mass declaring the antiquity of the place — but Leicester punched huge windows into it, dressing ancient strength in Elizabethan glass. And below the walls he laid out the privy garden: terraces, obelisks, an aviary of exotic birds, a marble fountain — recorded in such detail by an eyewitness that English Heritage rebuilt it in 2009. Around it all lay the mere, the vast lake that had made medieval Kenilworth almost siege-proof and that Leicester turned into a stage.

Notice what he did not build: nothing military. Like Acton Burnell three centuries earlier, Kenilworth in the 1570s shows defences repurposed as display — but here the purpose was sharper than status. Every stone was aimed at the queen’s opinion.

The Nineteen Days of 1575

Elizabeth had visited before — 1566, 1568, 1572 — but the visit of 9 to 27 July 1575 outdid everything in the reign: the longest stay she made at any courtier’s house. Leicester met her with a floating ‘Lady of the Lake’ welcoming her to a castle of legend; fireworks were reportedly heard twenty miles away; there was hunting by day and masques by night, bear-baiting, an Italian tumbler, and a swimming pageant in the mere where a performer as Arion, the legendary musician of Greek myth, rode a mechanical dolphin. Contemporaries claimed the entertainment cost Leicester a fortune — a figure of a thousand pounds a day was bandied about, and even if gossip inflated it, the true cost would have crushed most noble families. We know the detail because two eyewitness accounts survive: a long gossipy letter attributed to Robert Langham, a minor court official, and the poet George Gascoigne’s Princely Pleasures.

Most historians read 1575 as Leicester’s last grand bid for Elizabeth’s hand. The pageants said it almost openly — masques of marriage and of a lady released from an enchanted lake — and one planned entertainment pressing the theme was, tellingly, never performed; historians suspect the queen declined to hear it. She was forty-one, and hopes of the Leicester match were fading; and she left Kenilworth unmarried, as she left everywhere. For your exam, the visit is the marriage question (Lesson 3) staged in fireworks — and refused.

What the Site Shows About Elizabethan England

Kenilworth in 1575 is the court system working at full power. It shows how progresses let Elizabeth be seen by her people and fed at her courtiers’ expense — power displayed while someone else paid. It shows what favour was worth: a castle, offices and income flowed to Dudley, and he poured them back into loyalty spectacular enough for the whole kingdom to hear about. It shows the marriage question as living politics, played out in allegory before thousands. And it shows the propaganda machinery of the reign — poets, pageants and print carrying the event far beyond Warwickshire. The gossip, expense and spectacle of those nineteen days are as much a primary source for Elizabeth’s rule as any statute.

Key Fact

Two eyewitness accounts preserve the 1575 visit: the letter attributed to Robert Langham describing the festivities and the garden, and George Gascoigne’s Princely Pleasures at Kenilworth. Detail from the Langham letter guided English Heritage’s 2009 reconstruction of the Elizabethan garden.

The Site Afterwards and in the Exam

Leicester died in 1588, deep in debt. The castle passed on, was slighted after the Civil War in 1650 — the keep’s north side blown out, the mere drained — and settled into ruin. Today English Heritage keeps the shell, the gatehouse, the rebuilt garden and the empty basin of the mere. In the 16-mark question, chain features to meanings: Leicester’s Building → the cost of hosting the queen; the garden and pageants → courtship politics; the mere as stage → medieval strength repurposed as theatre; the gift of 1563 → how favour worked. Then weigh the site against your contextual knowledge of the court, progresses and the marriage question.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the work Leicester carried out at Kenilworth for Elizabeth's visits.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Leicester's Building — a four-storey block of state apartments lodging the queen in modern comfort beside the medieval hall.
• A grand new gatehouse giving arriving courtiers a fashionable first impression (it survives intact).
• Great windows cut into the twelfth-century keep, dressing medieval mass in Elizabethan glass.
• The privy garden below the walls — terraces, obelisks, aviary and fountain, rebuilt by English Heritage in 2009 from the Langham letter.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the entertainments staged at Kenilworth in July 1575.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Lady of the Lake pageant welcoming Elizabeth across the mere on her arrival.
• A swimming pageant with a performer as Arion riding a mechanical dolphin on the lake.
• Fireworks reportedly heard many miles away, masques by night and hunting by day.
• The sheer duration and cost — nineteen days, with gossip claiming a thousand pounds a day.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of royal progresses for Elizabeth's style of rule, using Kenilworth as your example.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Visibility: progresses displayed the queen to her subjects across the country — monarchy performed in person, with Kenilworth 1575 its most spectacular stage.
• Economy: courtiers bore the crushing cost of hosting, so the crown bought magnificence with favour instead of money.
• Control of the elite: the hope and expense of a visit kept nobles competing to demonstrate loyalty — Leicester rebuilt a castle for the privilege.
• Propaganda reach: printed accounts like Gascoigne's carried the spectacle far beyond those present.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of Elizabeth's visit to Kenilworth in July 1575.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Arrival, 9 July: greeted by pageantry including the Lady of the Lake welcoming her to the castle across the mere.
• The stay: nineteen days of hunting, bear-baiting, masques, fireworks heard at great distance, and the Arion water pageant on the lake.
• The subtext: entertainments of courtship and marriage, with one pressing entertainment never performed — read by most historians as Leicester's final bid for her hand.
• Departure, 27 July: the queen left unmarried; the visit passed into legend through the Langham letter and Gascoigne's Princely Pleasures.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of what the 1575 visit cost Leicester.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It measures what royal favour was worth pursuing: contemporaries spoke of a thousand pounds a day, on top of years of building — spending aimed at one listener.
• It shows the court economy: Elizabeth's gift of the castle in 1563 flowed back to her as hospitality — favour converted to loyalty and display.
• It shows the risk side of the system: Leicester died in 1588 heavily in debt; competitive magnificence could ruin even the greatest favourite.
• It strengthens the courtship reading: expenditure this extreme fits a suit for the queen's hand, not routine hospitality.

practice_questions.text: 'Kenilworth in 1575 shows that entertainment was really politics at Elizabeth's court.' How far does a study of Kenilworth support this statement? Explain your answer. You should refer to Kenilworth and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Support for the statement (site evidence):
• The pageants argued in allegory — the Lady of the Lake and marriage masques staged Leicester's suit; the unperformed entertainment suggests a message the queen declined to hear.
• The buildings themselves were political instruments: Leicester's Building and the garden existed to honour and persuade one guest.
• The scale of spending only makes sense as investment in favour — the currency of Elizabethan politics.
Against the statement (site evidence and context):
• Much of the programme was straightforward pleasure — hunting, fireworks, acrobats — the shared culture of the court rather than coded argument.
• The politics had limits: the spectacular suit failed; Elizabeth kept the marriage question unanswered here as everywhere, suggesting entertainment could ask but never decide.
• Progresses served purposes beyond courtship — royal visibility and the display of a loyal, orderly realm.
A developed judgement on how far pleasure and politics can be separated at this court is required for the top level.
